# The Worker Process and Client Frontends {#sec-frontends}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

So far, every chapter has been about what runs *inside* the engine.
This chapter is about how a user gets queries *into* the engine —
through what processes, over what protocols, in what shape.

Three pieces:

- **`nes-single-node-worker`** — the worker process. A long-running
  binary that listens for queries, executes them, and reports
  status. This is where the engine actually lives.
- **`nes-frontend/apps/cli`** — a non-interactive CLI for
  submitting queries from a script.
- **`nes-frontend/apps/repl`** — an interactive REPL,
  conventionally called `nes-repl`.

All three communicate over gRPC. We will walk through each.

---

## 18.1 The worker process {#sec-worker-process}

The worker binary is `nes-single-node-worker`. Its main entry
point lives in `nes-single-node-worker/src/SingleNodeWorker.cpp`.
On startup it:

1. Reads its configuration (file path or CLI args).
2. Constructs a `BufferManager`, an `ExecutableQueryPlan`
   compiler, a `QueryEngine`, and the catalogs.
3. Calls `registerAll` on each plugin registry to populate them.
4. Starts the gRPC server on (default) localhost:8080.
5. Waits for queries.

The single class `SingleNodeWorker` orchestrates the engine's
core. Its main public surface is the `registerQuery` method:

```cpp
// nes-single-node-worker/src/SingleNodeWorker.cpp (sketch)
std::expected<QueryId, Exception>
SingleNodeWorker::registerQuery(LogicalPlan plan) noexcept
{
    if (plan.getQueryId() == INVALID_QUERY_ID) {
        std::uniform_int_distribution<size_t> dist(
            QueryId::INITIAL,
            std::numeric_limits<int32_t>::max());
        plan.setQueryId(QueryId(dist(*idGenerator.wlock())));
    }
    auto request = std::make_unique<QueryCompilation::QueryCompilationRequest>(plan);
    auto result = compiler->compileQuery(std::move(request));
    // ... store the compiled plan, return the query id ...
}
```

The function takes a `LogicalPlan` (already parsed and bound by
the client) and returns either a `QueryId` (success) or an
`Exception` (failed compilation). The compiled plan is stored in
the engine's catalog; subsequent `startQuery` and `stopQuery`
calls reference it by `QueryId`.

The worker is a single-process, multi-threaded design. There is
no daemon-and-workers split inside a single worker. One
`nes-single-node-worker` process can run as a stand-alone engine
(everything in one process) or as one node in a distributed
deployment, where multiple workers are coordinated by a
separate Rust coordinator (Chapter 19). The gRPC API on port
8080 is the same in both modes; the only difference is whether
the worker is reachable to *other* workers via the
`nes-network` channels.

---

## 18.2 The gRPC service {#sec-grpc-service}

The gRPC service is in
`nes-single-node-worker/include/GrpcService.hpp`. The service
definition:

```cpp
// nes-single-node-worker/include/GrpcService.hpp
class GRPCServer final : public WorkerRPCService::Service {
public:
    grpc::Status RegisterQuery(grpc::ServerContext*,
                               const RegisterQueryRequest*,
                               RegisterQueryReply*) override;
    grpc::Status StartQuery(grpc::ServerContext*,
                            const StartQueryRequest*,
                            google::protobuf::Empty*) override;
    grpc::Status StopQuery(grpc::ServerContext*,
                           const StopQueryRequest*,
                           google::protobuf::Empty*) override;
    grpc::Status RequestQueryStatus(grpc::ServerContext*,
                                    const QueryStatusRequest*,
                                    QueryStatusReply*) override;
    grpc::Status RequestStatus(grpc::ServerContext*,
                               const WorkerStatusRequest*,
                               WorkerStatusResponse*) override;
    explicit GRPCServer(SingleNodeWorker&& delegate)
        : delegate(std::move(delegate)) { }
private:
    SingleNodeWorker delegate;
};
```

Five methods. `RegisterQuery` accepts a serialised `LogicalPlan`
and returns a `QueryId`. `StartQuery` and `StopQuery` are
identifier-only operations. `RequestQueryStatus` returns the
state of a single query (registered, running, stopped, failed).
`RequestStatus` returns engine-wide health (active queries,
buffer utilisation, etc.).

The proto definitions live in `grpc/`:

- `SingleNodeWorkerRPCService.proto` — the service interface.
- `SerializableQueryPlan.proto` — the wire format for
  `LogicalPlan`. Logical plans are not directly serialised C++
  objects; they go through this proto encoding.
- `SerializableDataType.proto` — the wire format for `DataType`
  and `Schema`.

The proto encoding means the parser and binder run *on the client*,
not the worker. The worker receives a fully-bound logical plan and
proceeds straight to optimisation. We will see why this matters
in @sec-where-bind.

---

## 18.3 Where binding happens {#sec-where-bind}

A query in NebulaStream is bound on the client side, not the
server side. The client (the REPL or the CLI) parses the SQL,
binds against its local copy of the source/sink catalog, and sends
the worker a serialised `LogicalPlan`.

This is unusual. Most database systems bind on the server, where
the catalog lives authoritatively. NebulaStream's choice flips the
arrangement: the catalog is conceptually authoritative on the
worker (it owns the engine's running state), but binding can run
on either side because catalog updates flow both ways via gRPC.

The benefit is that the gRPC API can ingest fully-typed plans
with no further validation needed. The cost is that the client
needs a recent view of the catalog. In the single-node deployment
we have today, the cost is essentially zero (catalog is local to
the same machine). In a future distributed deployment, the cost
becomes non-trivial — the catalog has to be replicated to wherever
the binding happens.

---

## 18.4 The REPL {#sec-repl}

The interactive front-end is `nes-frontend/apps/repl`. The class
is `Repl`, in `nes-frontend/apps/repl/Repl.hpp`:

```cpp
// nes-frontend/apps/repl/Repl.hpp (sketch)
class Repl {
public:
    Repl(SourceStatementHandler&,
         SinkStatementHandler&,
         TopologyStatementHandler&,
         QueryStatementHandler&,
         StatementBinder&,
         ErrorBehaviour,
         OutputFormat,
         InteractiveMode,
         std::stop_token);
    void run();
private:
    struct Impl;
    std::unique_ptr<Impl> pImpl;
};
```

The `Repl` is a Pimpl-shaped class — its private state lives
behind a `unique_ptr<Impl>` to keep the header light. The
constructor takes one handler per statement kind (source, sink,
topology, query) plus a binder, plus configuration.

`run` is the main loop: read a line, parse, bind, dispatch to
the appropriate handler. The handler talks to the worker over
gRPC. Output is formatted according to the configured `OutputFormat`
(table, CSV, JSON).

The REPL is the user's typical entry point. It accepts the same
SQL as the CLI; the only difference is interactivity.

---

## 18.5 The CLI {#sec-cli}

The non-interactive CLI is `nes-frontend/apps/cli`, conventionally
called `nebuli`. The starter is in
`nes-frontend/apps/cli/CLIStarter.cpp`. Its job is the same as the
REPL's, minus the readline loop: read SQL from stdin or a file,
bind, submit, exit.

The CLI is what scripts use. The README's demo query is exercised
end-to-end through it:

```shell
cmake-build-debug/nes-frontend/apps/cli/nebuli -s localhost:8080 < demo.sql
```

`nebuli`'s output is conventionally CSV-formatted (one row per
result tuple); the REPL defaults to a table format. Both can be
overridden.

---

## 18.6 The configuration system {#sec-configurations}

A short note on the infrastructure that all of the above is
configured through. The `nes-configurations/` module supplies
a small visitor-based configuration framework — `BaseConfiguration`
and a family of typed options (`ScalarOption`, `EnumOption`,
`SequenceOption`) plus validators (`IpValidation`,
`BooleanValidation`, etc.). Both command-line flags and YAML
configuration files map onto the same option tree, so a worker
configuration that lives in a YAML file can be overridden on
the command line with no syntactic difference.

This is what `--worker.default_query_execution.execution_mode=INTERPRETER`
in our exercises throughout the book actually does: walks the
`SingleNodeWorkerConfiguration` tree and sets one
`EnumOption<ExecutionMode>` leaf. The same mechanism powers the
coordinator's configuration in distributed deployments
(Chapter 19).

The dependence on a generic configuration framework rather
than ad-hoc parsing makes it cheap to add new options as the
engine grows; almost every chapter that has introduced a
"configurable" concept (buffer pool size, watermark slack,
network thread count) is plumbed through this same machinery.

## 18.7 Topology statements (and what they hint at) {#sec-topology}

The REPL's constructor mentions a `TopologyStatementHandler`. This
is for statements like `SHOW TOPOLOGY` and (eventually) `ATTACH
NODE`, `DETACH NODE` — statements that interact with the engine's
topology rather than its data flow.

In the single-node deployment we have today, these statements are
mostly no-ops or query the trivially-trivial single-node topology.
In a future distributed deployment, they would be the user's
window into the engine's topology graph.

We mention them here because they are the only piece of the
front-end that points at the engine's distributed future. We will
have more to say about that future in Chapter 19.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch18-summary}

NebulaStream's worker is a single C++ process (`nes-single-node-worker`)
exposing five gRPC methods: register, start, stop, query status,
worker status. Two client frontends — an interactive REPL
(`nes-repl`) and a non-interactive CLI (`nebuli`) — speak to the
worker over the same gRPC API. Binding happens client-side; the
worker receives fully-typed `LogicalPlan`s. The architecture is
deliberately flat: no separate coordinator, no daemon-workers
split; one process is the engine.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch18-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 18.1: end-to-end demo"}
Run the README's demo query end-to-end. Use `nes-repl` as
client, `nes-single-node-worker` as server. Verify the round-
trip: SQL in, CSV out. Where in the worker's log do you see the
`RegisterQuery` arrive? Where do you see the first `WorkTask`
emitted? Where does the file source's first read happen?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 18.2: speak gRPC directly"}
Use `grpcurl` (or the equivalent in your language of choice) to
hit the worker's `RequestStatus` endpoint directly:

```shell
grpcurl -plaintext -d '{}' localhost:8080 \
    nes.proto.WorkerRPCService/RequestStatus
```

You should get back a status structure. Identify the fields:
how many queries are running? How is the worker's health
reported?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 18.3: client-side binding"}
Modify a small `nes-repl` invocation to use a source name that
exists on the client but does not exist on the worker. Does
the binder error before the gRPC call, or does the worker
reject the plan? Trace through the code to confirm.
:::
